S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform, typically aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing a feared event. The obsessions and compulsions are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and the individual usually recognizes that these behaviors or thoughts are excessive or unreasonable. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood but can occur later in life, and the course is frequently chronic with waxing and waning severity, often exacerbated by stress. OCD is distinguished from psychotic disorders by preserved insight, and from generalized anxiety or obsessive–compulsive personality traits by the presence of specific, ritualized responses to clearly demarcated intrusive thoughts rather than a diffuse pattern of worry or enduring perfectionism.

patient.personality: Margaret is a highly analytical, risk-averse engineer who thrives on order and precision, often channeling that same structured mindset into her hobbies and tending to over-schedule herself while neglecting self-care.
patient.stressor: In the years leading up to her early forties, Margaret was placed in charge of a high-profile launch vehicle project where even minor design errors could have catastrophic consequences, coinciding with a period of corporate restructuring that thinned out her support team. As deadlines tightened and responsibility for safety-critical decisions increasingly rested on her shoulders, she began staying later and later at work, feeling personally accountable for preventing any potential failure, and she started developing increasingly involved routines around how she reviewed calculations and documentation. What initially seemed like thoroughness gradually became an inflexible pattern of repetitive cross-checking and mental rehearsing that she felt compelled to complete to feel that designs were “truly safe,” spilling over into her home life as she ritualized planning, scheduling, and even simple household tasks, crowding out sleep, hiking, and time for friends. She sought psychiatric care after missing a major internal deadline because she was stuck in her own cycles of re-verification, and her manager gently confronted her about how her need to repeat certain review steps was now jeopardizing both the project timeline and her ability to function as a team lead.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’ve started getting caught in these drawn-out checking routines at work and at home, repeating the same steps so many times that it’s derailing my day.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: All day, especially when I’m tired or under pressure, my mind keeps ambushing me with these “what if I missed something tiny and the rocket explodes” scenarios, and no matter how many times I remind myself we’ve met every safety margin, I can’t shut off the looping images of bolts shearing and fuel tanks rupturing because of some imaginary decimal point I supposedly overlooked.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: To quiet that fear, I end up rereading the same pages of calculations or design specs over and over, tracing each line with my finger or re-running the numbers in my head until it “feels” safe, and I do the same thing at home—checking the stove knobs in a set pattern, rewriting my to‑do lists multiple times—so that what should be a five‑minute task can swallow an entire evening before I can move on.
